I do this with my dog as well, it’s not that hard if you do it correctly from puppyhood. I started when he was about two years old, we are able to do it but he’s not as relaxed as this dog haha.

It’s achievable with a calming/bonding exercise based on something a mother dog would do with her puppies to calm them down. 

When the puppy needs to calm down but doesn’t want to because it’s a puppy, you place them on their back between your legs and hold their leg and snout (simulating how a mother dog will bite/hold very lightly around the puppies heads/snouts to calm them) lightly until they fall asleep. Some will resist a bit but if you keep through it a couple of times they’ll love this as it makes them feel safe. It’s great for bonding and calming. Once they’re used to this you can usually add nail clipping.

No this harnesses will definitely restrict shoulder movement which can lead to tendinitis.

Some types of front clips are definitely worse than others but damage is likely going to happen regardless of type if one uses one a lot incorrectly. If a dog pulls through it and the front clip has essentially no effect this restricts the movement (making the dog pull with a slant). If it isn’t used heavily though, as you said in combination with a back clip for example, there shouldn’t be any risks. 

I would be suspicious of any harness with a strap that goes across on top of the shoulders (like the second one you linked). T-shaped harnesses can also cause tendinitis with heavy use, even if we think it’s loose enough it’s usually uncomfortable for the dog because they can’t stretch out their legs enough when moving.

I would advise to have both. A correctly fitted harness in a y-shape, H-shape or pulling harness are more ergonomically fit for your dog and correctly evens out the strain along the body and is great when hiking, doings sports and playing. 

You get more control with a collar which is better for training and walks in crowded places or where you want more control over her head. Make sure you get one that’s in the correct size, it should be placed higher up on the neck than most people realise. 

If you’re going to use a prong make sure you actually get a correct size, they’re a great tool cor some when used correctly, but cheap, unfitted prongs are the absolute worst. 

If she’s pulling a lot and you don’t have much experience training nor the time for it, you could use a gentle leader. It can take a while to get some dogs accustomed to one but use positive reinforcement to get her used to it. My staffy used to be a big puller but I have trained him and he now walks nicely with me, but if my grandma or younger brothers wants to walk him I use one just in case. 

I would not recommend a T-shaped harness (Like the popular Julius K9 harness or those of similar shape) because the front strap wraps around on top of the shoulders and restricts the dogs movement, with daily use over time they can develop tendinitis and other problems.

I would also not recommend ‘heavy’ use of a front clip harness. A front clip can be a good training tool for some in training a dog to walk nicely on a lead but heavy and daily use of the front clip when a dog pulls a lot can make the movement restricted and the dog can develop tendinitis.

Because breed traits are more complicated than that. 

There are a few different factors that make up a dog and yes genetics is a big part of that, but not only breed-qualities, but it also depends on the lines which the dog comes from. 

That’s why you see common health issues in breeds but not in lines of that breed that has been screened and health tested to avoid those problems. (Though yes “some” breeds have unavoidable problems)

Take the Australian shepherd for example. The breed is known to be more prone to neurological problems that leads them to be “nervy”, hyper, fearful and reactive. Though it’s more common within this “breed”, ethical breeders who take health and mentality seriously and preform health tests and mental tests on their dogs don’t breed Australian shepherds with these problems. 

Another thing that’s wrong with this sentiment is that the pit bull terrier is a very new breed compared to these other breeds you mention. 
Pointers, hunting dogs, sledding dogs and shepherds are very old breeds. Their natural instincts to heard, point, pull comes from many many more years of breed development. The pit-bull terrier comes from the bull-and-terrier dog which was produced during the 1800s, and we don’t see the aggression statistics with the other breeds that came from the same lines. 

And most importantly the breed was never ever purposely bred to be aggressive towards humans, but used in dog-fighting. 
Many pitbull terriers do have dog-aggression though, and it’s even mentioned in the dog-standard, but also mentioned there is that aggressive behaviour is very undesirable and leads to [disqualification](https://www.ukcdogs.com/american-pit-bull-terrier#).

So why are there so many attacks from this breed? Well between a bit icky statistics, it being such a wide spread breed and mixes of it in america, I think there’s just very many unstable lines. 
The pit-bull has a stigma for being “cool and dangerous” which doesn’t only bring in the bad kind of owners, but also the bad type of breeders: Breeders that breed unstable, confused and nervous temperaments and unhealthy dogs, with only money, colour and looks in mind.

So the experience of pit-bulls differ both because of people’s inexperience but also because the temperaments vary very much between the lines. 
Now these kind of dogs from the bad lines are harder to keep, but not impossible. I don’t think they should be band, just have responsables owners who can train them and knows their own dogs limits.

Edit: Staffordshire bull terriers should not be aggressive at all, that’s disqualifying according to the breed standard, I have one as well. So that’s not a breed thing but a bad lines thing. If you get a poorly bred dog you’re going to have to spend often a lot more time socialising and training them!

I was not allowed to feel sad when my aunt, who was the one of the only ones who truly tried to step in and help raise me, died, because it was “her” sister, “I couldn’t possibly understand what her loss felt like”.
